clue.text: Fly like some insects, or bat

blocks.note: first meaning: to flap the wings quickly and lightly
second meaning: to bat one's eyelashes, moving them rapidly

explanation.walkthrough: 'bat' looks like the flying mammal, a natural partner for insects, but it is the verb used of eyelashes.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb describes quick flapping movement, whether of an insect's wings in flight or of eyelids batted coquettishly.

clue.text: Inflict corporal punishment on kid, for example

blocks.note: first meaning: thrash, as with a strap
second meaning: a material, as kid is goatskin

explanation.walkthrough: Kid looks like a child being punished, but it is the soft skin of a young goat.
explanation.definitionFit: To leather someone is to beat them, and kid is one type of tanned animal hide.

clue.text: Start of tribute about stupid Italian poet

indicators.note: surrounding the next word, so it goes inside

blocks.note: a dedicated tribute begins with the word 'To ...'
an ass is a stupid person

explanation.surface: A tribute to an Italian poet opens by calling him a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start of tribute' is not just T: a dedication starts with the word TO, which wraps around the fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Torquato Tasso was a sixteenth-century Italian poet, author of Jerusalem Delivered.

clue.text: Passing white's soaring over grass

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading upward, back to front

blocks.note: white as in pale, with the 's meaning is
to grass is slang for to inform on, as is to sing

explanation.surface: A white ball passing high over a lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Grass means turn informer here, not lawn. Over in a down clue puts the first part above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that is elapsing is passing by.

clue.text: Like husband found in a fornicating situation?

definitions.text: Like husband found in a fornicating situation?

indicators.note: something found in a place sits inside it, so the first pieces go within the last

blocks.note: like = as, in comparisons
H is the standard abbreviation for husband
a bed, where such activity takes place

explanation.surface: A husband caught in bed with his lover would look a certain way.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: AS H goes inside A BED, and a husband so discovered would surely be embarrassed.
explanation.definitionFit: Abashed means embarrassed and ashamed, exactly how a husband caught in flagrante would feel.

clue.text: Add fatty stuff to heart of cabbage, say

indicators.note: the heart is the very centre, so only the middle letter is kept

blocks.note: the central letter of the seven
to utter is to say

explanation.surface: A cook enriching the centre of a cabbage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart of cabbage' reads as the vegetable's core, but it is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To butter is to spread butter, a fatty food, on something.

clue.text: Put in situation hard to get out of? Possibly, providing one red's OK

definitions.text: Put in situation hard to get out of?

indicators.note: possibly signals one of several possible arrangements of the letters

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A snooker player hoping one red ball is safe.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's red ball belongs to the game whose name the answer echoes; in snooker you must pot a red first.
explanation.definitionFit: To be snookered is to be left in a position with no easy way out, from the game's blocked shot.

clue.text: Ambassador's immersed in European matter in Greek city

indicators.note: something immersed in a substance is surrounded by it

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
matter as in discharge from a wound
HE, His Excellency, an ambassador's title, plus S for is

explanation.surface: A diplomat engrossed in European affairs in a Greek town.
explanation.walkthrough: Matter here is pus, not affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Ephesus was an ancient Greek city on the Ionian coast, now in Turkey.

clue.text: Endlessly distrust the writer taken in by penchant for verbal ambiguity

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter is dropped
taken in means swallowed inside the next word

blocks.note: to doubt is to distrust
a leaning is an inclination
the writer refers to the setter: me

explanation.surface: A writer's fondness for ambiguity breeds endless mistrust.
explanation.definitionFit: A double meaning is a phrase open to two interpretations, which is verbal ambiguity.

clue.text: Food in repast is oddly deficient

indicators.note: lacking in the odd positions, so only the even-numbered letters remain

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A meal said to be oddly lacking in nourishment.
explanation.walkthrough: Repast hints at the food but the definition is the first word; the letters come from repast and is read together.
explanation.definitionFit: Eats is an informal noun for food, as in a sign offering cheap eats.

clue.text: Mark similar to 18, but higher

blocks.note: surface reading: a grade or score close to another but a bit better
setter's reading: a punctuation mark shaped like the answer to 18 but written up at letter height

explanation.surface: A score close to eighteen, but a little better.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is COMMA; the apostrophe has the same shape but sits raised above the line.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostrophe is a punctuation sign identical in form to a comma, placed high rather than on the baseline.

clue.text: Snaps emerging branches

blocks.note: first meaning: takes photographs
second meaning: new growth sprouting from a plant

explanation.walkthrough: Snaps could be breaks, suiting branches, but here it means photographs. This answer also belongs to the panda joke with 10 and 22.
explanation.definitionFit: To shoot is to photograph, and shoots are young stems growing out from a plant.

clue.text: Maximally exposed, first covering up hole

indicators.note: a cover goes around what it hides, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: first-placed, the best
a leak is a hole letting something escape

explanation.surface: Something at its most exposed whose first job is hiding a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Bleak describes a bare, windswept place, so the superlative is the most exposed to the elements.

clue.text: Minded after power is handed over

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for power
minded as in objected to

explanation.surface: Someone objected once power was transferred to another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' puts the power letter in front of the word for minded.
explanation.definitionFit: To present something is to give it formally, so presented means handed over.

clue.text: A point above 18 in game before final pass forward

blocks.note: the semi-final
a col is a mountain pass
on as in onward

explanation.surface: Scoring a point in a semi-final with a forward pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is COMMA: the semicolon is a dot over a comma. The sporting surface hides a mountain pass.
explanation.definitionFit: The semicolon is drawn as a full stop placed directly over a comma.

clue.text: Secure arms from Communist Russia

indicators.note: taken from the run of letters across these words, sitting inside them

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Acquiring weapons from the Soviet Union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secure arms' reads as obtaining weapons, but it means tying someone's arms to their body.
explanation.definitionFit: To truss is to bind someone tightly, typically with arms pinned to the sides.

clue.text: Rowdy drunk driver admitting nothing

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: a driver is a user of a car
zero

explanation.surface: A loud drunk-driver confessing to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Rowdy drunk is a noun phrase here, not a description of the driver.
explanation.definitionFit: A carouser is someone who drinks and revels noisily.

clue.text: One among 6, 25 amalgamated, or what divides them

blocks.note: first meaning: a species of the insects named by joining 6 and 25
second meaning: the punctuation sign printed between the 6 and the 25

explanation.walkthrough: 6 and 25 are BUTTER and FLIES; joined they make butterflies, and the comma is a butterfly with ragged wings. The mark between 6 and 25 in the clue is also a comma.
explanation.definitionFit: The comma is both a British butterfly species and the punctuation mark that separates items in a list.

clue.text: Put out eggs – almost leave out scrambled

indicators.note: not quite all, so the last letter goes
scrambled means jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the two words together, whose final E of the first is then dropped

explanation.surface: Instructions for eggs: nearly leave them out, scrambled.
explanation.walkthrough: Scrambled eggs is the cookery picture, but scrambled is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To ovulate is to release an egg cell from the ovary.

clue.text: Monarch displayed in museum – initially housed show in ground-floor extensions

indicators.note: an exhibit displayed in a gallery sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other
at the start, so only the opening letter of each following word is used

blocks.note: the V&A, London's Victoria and Albert Museum, written out as V AND A
ER, Elizabeth Regina
the rest of V AND A
opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A royal exhibition at a museum, staged in single-storey annexes.
explanation.walkthrough: The V&A is the Victoria and Albert Museum in London; spelling the ampersand as AND gives the letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: A verandah is a roofed open gallery built onto the ground floor of a house.

clue.text: It's not easy catching variety, American counterpart of 24

indicators.note: catching means holding inside

blocks.note: not easy is hard
VAR is the abbreviation for variety

explanation.surface: Something difficult to grasp: diversity in an American setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 is OXFORD, England's ancient university.
explanation.definitionFit: Harvard is America's oldest and most prestigious university, much as Oxford is in England.

clue.text: Doesn't finish some panda food

blocks.note: first meaning
second meaning: foliage, part of a panda's diet

explanation.walkthrough: With 10 and 12 this completes the punctuation joke 'Eats, shoots and leaves', about a panda whose comma turns its diet into a gunfight.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave food is not to finish it, and leaves are foliage that pandas eat along with bamboo shoots.

clue.text: Invariably costly meal, it's said, extended by indefinite period

blocks.note: from the saying that there's no such thing as a free one
an eon is an immeasurably long age

explanation.surface: A proverbially expensive meal that drags on endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's said' points to the proverb 'there's no such thing as a free lunch', not to a sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A luncheon is a formal midday meal, the longer version of the everyday word.

clue.text: Kind of 18, or kind of blue

blocks.note: first meaning: the serial comma before 'and' in a list
second meaning: a dark navy shade

explanation.walkthrough: 18 is COMMA, and the Oxford comma is the one before the final 'and'. Oxford blue is a dark blue, also the sporting colours awarded at the university.
explanation.definitionFit: The university city's name qualifies both a style of comma and a deep shade of blue.

clue.text: Is highly moving in theatre part

blocks.note: first meaning: travels through the air
second meaning: the space above a stage where scenery is hung

explanation.walkthrough: 'Highly moving' suggests emotion; it means moving high up.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that flies moves through the air, and the flies are the loft above a theatre stage.

clue.text: Flits with dashing young men around small Roman square

indicators.note: the young men stand around the square, enclosing it

blocks.note: gallants are stylish, chivalrous young men
four in Roman numerals, the square of two and a small one

explanation.surface: Someone flirting with handsome youths in an Italian piazza.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small Roman square' looks like a little piazza in Rome, but it is a square number written as a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: To gallivant is to roam about in search of pleasure, much as to flit is to move lightly from place to place.

clue.text: Tyrannical ruler found in previous answer, after all

indicators.note: only a part found inside the longer word is kept, the rest discarded

blocks.note: the answer just before this one, at 26

explanation.surface: A despot discovered in the last solution after all.
explanation.walkthrough: In GALLIVANTS the ruler comes straight after the letters ALL, so 'after all' is literally true. Ivan the Terrible was the tyrannical Russian tsar.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan IV of Russia, known as the Terrible, is the archetypal tyrant tsar.

clue.text: Originality of points, three of them in all

indicators.note: one set placed in another, inside it

blocks.note: all four compass points
three of the compass points

explanation.surface: How novel some points are, counting three overall.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter is a compass point: three of them sit inside all four.
explanation.definitionFit: Newness is the quality of being new, which is what originality means.

clue.text: Conservative regret about pathetic campaign

indicators.note: lying about something means surrounding it, so one word wraps the next

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
to rue is to regret
sad as in pitiful

explanation.surface: A Tory laments a feeble political campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusade is a vigorous campaign for a cause, a sense extended from the medieval religious wars.
